response.answer: The SUSAN Electrofan must evaluate takeoff, climb, and off-nominal engine-failure profiles because cruise is not necessarily the limiting design condition. Takeoff and climb, along with failure cases, can be bounding factors in design optimization, while engine failures may have an especially large effect on sizing for novel aircraft configurations. Mission profiles therefore establish sizing requirements and performance constraints, including aircraft size, endurance, and range. Defining these profiles against airworthiness standards also supports certification by helping ensure that predicted performance remains compliant with applicable regulations throughout the design process.

Mission profiles define aircraft-state and flight-characteristic requirements that serve as sizing constraints and help establish aircraft size, endurance, and range.
Defining mission profiles within airworthiness certification standards helps designers maintain compliance with applicable regulations and standards during conceptual design.

response.answer: After a tail-mounted turbofan failure at or above VEF, SUSAN is assumed to continue using only its electric propulsion system, powered by the backup battery. The aircraft would climb at a reduced rate and then cruise at reduced altitude and speed, allowing a safe landing within a maximum 300-nautical-mile range. For preliminary OEI sizing, the electric engines are required to provide 7.2 MW throughout the climb to safe altitude. This is not simply 65% of the normal power: the 65/35 split describes cruise thrust—65% from the distributed electric propulsion system and 35% from the turbofan—whereas the OEI case assumes the turbofan is unavailable and requires the electric system to supply the full 7.2 MW. The 7.2 MW value comes from taking half of the estimated 14.4 MW, 100%-power normal climb requirement derived from the Boeing 737 MAX 8 comparison. The sizing conservatively uses 100% power, although actual OEI maximum-continuous power may be lower because of engine limitations; the applicable OEI criteria and additional electric-propulsion failure cases would require regulatory agreement and demonstration.

claims.text: Following loss of the single tail-mounted turbofan, the assumed worst-case OEI operation uses only electric propulsion, with the backup battery supplying the electrical power; the battery is sized to support takeoff power requirements.

SUSAN is assumed to meet the OEI objective with a reduced climb rate, followed by reduced-altitude and reduced-speed operation that provides time for a safe landing, with a stated maximum flight range of 300 nautical miles.
For preliminary sizing, the electric engines must provide 7.2 MW for the duration of the OEI climb to safe altitude.

The 65/35 split applies to cruise thrust: 65% is supplied by the wing-mounted electric engines and 35% by the fuel-burning turbofan. With the turbofan lost, the electric system must instead supply the full OEI requirement rather than only its cruise-share percentage.

The 7.2 MW sizing basis is half of the estimated 14.4 MW 100%-power climb requirement inferred from the Boeing 737 MAX 8 comparison, corresponding to the assumed OEI share of the normal two-engine climb power.

Using 100% power for the OEI sizing is explicitly conservative because actual maximum-continuous OEI power may be lower due to engine limitations; the applicable OEI requirement and additional degraded distributed-electric-propulsion failure cases would need to be addressed with civil authorities.
